“Welcome to the Philippines,” she told Mr. Trump. She handed him a gift and blew him a kiss as he walked away with her son.

“She’s always the most beautiful,” Mr. Trump remarked.

Ms. Marcos wielded immense power when her husband was president and came to be known for her flamboyant lifestyle, shoe collection and unexplained wealth.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Trump, who was in the Philippines for a brief state visit, has made clear that he admires the Marcos family, part of his well-known affinity for autocratic leaders. On Tuesday night, he said to Mr. Marcos: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great.” He went on, “I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”.

In a recent development, earlier on Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila that Trump was willing to meet with Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, to resolve issues. However, Rubio did not say whether a meeting between Trump and Kim was likely to happen.

Industry observers note that “The president has never viewed meeting and talking to someone as a concession,” Rubio said. “How are you going to solve problems with people you have disagreements with if you don’t speak to them?”.

In a recent development, xi’s decision to personally greet Trump at the airport is unusual. He did not come himself when Trump visited Beijing in May. But Trump made a point of going to Joint Base Andrews outside Washington to greet Xi in September, a rare move for any American president and the first time Trump had done so for a foreign visitor.

Trump was greeted upon his arrival in Shenzhen by Xi, in an unusually high-level welcome ceremony. Foreign leaders are usually received by senior Chinese officials, not Xi himself.

Sources indicate that president Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines stated on Wednesday that he had fried chicken delivered to President Trump during his overnight stay in Manila.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t just any fried chicken. It came from Jollibee, a chain that is considered a national treasure in the Philippines.

Industry observers note that “Since you’re strapped for time, I thought a taste of Manila might be good. So last night, I asked my staff to have some Jollibee delivered as a late night snack for you and your delegation,” Mr. Marcos remarked in his remarks before a meeting with Mr. Trump.

Sources indicate that it was not clear if Mr. Trump actually ate any.

Mr. Marcos’s gesture was not only a matter of national pride, but also appeared to be a nod to Mr. Trump’s well-documented fondness for fast food. Mr. Trump, a self-described germaphobe, has said that he favors fast food from chains like McDonald’s because of their speed, consistency and hygiene.

In April, he received two McDonald’s bags delivered by DoorDash to the Oval Office, in an event the White House had staged to promote a Trump administration initiative that removed taxes on overtime and tips.

Industry observers note that “I like cleanliness, and I think you’re better off going there than maybe someplace that you have no idea where the food’s coming from. It’s a certain standard,” Mr. Trump said in a 2016 interview with CNN. Later that year, he posted a photo of himself on social media enjoying a bucket of Kentucky Fried Chicken on his private plane.

Mr. Marcos told Mr. Trump on Wednesday that Jollibee had surpassed Kentucky Fried Chicken in popularity in the United States. The claim was dubious but Mr. Trump replied: “Oh, wow, fantastic.”.

While KFC still has many more stores than Jollibee in the United States, the Filipino chain has promoted its fried chicken as America’s best since at least 2022, citing food critics’ rankings and three consecutive wins in a USA Today readers’ poll.

On its home turf, Jollibee far outpaces American fast-food chains in store count and revenue. To compete with Jollibee in the Philippines, McDonald’s has altered its local menu to offer a sweeter hamburger sauce, fried chicken and rice, and Filipino-style sweet spaghetti.

Jollibee has expanded beyond the Philippines by acquiring food brands in countries such as the United States, China and South Korea, including the Colorado-based burger chain Smashburger and the Hong Kong dim sum chain Tim Ho Wan.

Mr. Marcos’s shout-out came as Jollibee is exploring a Hong Kong Stock Exchange listing for its international business, after initially saying it would list in the United States. The firm’s founder and chairman, Tony Tan Caktiong, said in September that the change reflected Asian investors’ familiarity with the brand.

Jollibee has not opened any stores in Washington, though there are several in New York, Mr. Trump’s home state, and Florida, where he spends a lot of time.

Xi mentioned in a meeting with Putin that relations between China and Russia have remained as “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain,” according to Chinese state media. Xi called for the two sides to advance “world multipolarity” and the “democratization of international relations,” terms Xi uses to describe a world order in which the United States is less dominant.

At a lunch with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines on Wednesday, Trump noted that the two countries had unexpectedly signed a upcoming trade deal. Marcos’s office later said that the deal would cover energy and food security, without providing further details.

Recent findings suggest that “We didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both,” Trump said during the lunch. He later said on social media that the deal would benefit American farmers.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada told reporters that he would meet with Trump on Wednesday in Shenzhen to discuss the trade dispute between the two countries.

China warned on Tuesday that it could hit back after the Trump administration this week proposed a rule that would restrict China’s access to advanced chips through data centers outside its borders.

It has been revealed that china’s ministry of commerce said the rule went against the terms that China and the United States had agreed to in a fragile truce that expires in two months. “If the US persists, China will take countermeasures,” a ministry spokesman said.

China experts warned that the rule, the latest in a series of escalatory moves from both sides, would make it harder for Xi and Trump to come to any meaningful agreement to deescalate conflict between the world’s biggest economies.

It has been revealed that in a sign of Putin’s importance to Xi, the Russian leader was greeted at the airport in Shenzhen on Wednesday by Cai Qi, one of the seven members of the elite Politburo Standing Committee. That appears to make Cai the highest-ranking official to greet a foreign leader at APEC so far ahead of Trump’s arrival, according to a review of Chinese state media.

Sources indicate that cai is considered one of the most influential figures in Xi’s inner circle, having served as a deputy to the Chinese leader when he was a provincial official. He accompanied Xi to Washington in September.

According to recent reports, this is not the first time Cai has welcomed a foreign leader on the tarmac. Last year, he and Wang Yi, China’s top diplomat, greeted North Korea’s Kim Jong-un when he landed in Beijing.

Putin and Xi are expected to tour the campus that Moscow State University, Russia’s top university, set up in Shenzhen with the Beijing Institute of Technology. The leaders agreed to establish it a decade ago. The Shenzhen outpost looks like a mini version of the Moscow university, complete with a replica of its Stalin-era tower.

Putin and his team held talks with Xi followed by a smaller working breakfast. They have met dozens of times; this is at least their fourth in-person meeting this year. The talks lasted more than two hours, according to the Russian state news agency Tass.

World leaders coming to Shenzhen this week are arriving in an almost spotless, ultramodern metropolis, its streets bedecked with pastel banners but mostly emptied of the crowds typical of many Chinese cities.

Shenzhen lies slightly closer to the Equator than Havana, providing a balmy venue for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering. Under sunny skies with mild temperatures, a festive mood prevails in the city, which bears a strong resemblance to Miami — only much larger and with taller, newer high-rises.

Schools in Shenzhen have closed this week, many residents have left town and local authorities have instructed companies to allow those employees who are still here to work from home. The result has been a holiday atmosphere of sorts in a city with a tech sector known for its punishing “996” work schedules: 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.

Youthful volunteers — mainly students at local universities — stand on street corners wearing bright red vests, having been offered academic credit in exchange for being trained as guides. Thousands of gawkers have been promenading past the large conference center that will host heads of state from across the Asia Pacific region, taking photos of themselves in front of the flower gardens inside the fence.

In a recent development, among the crowds walking outside the high steel fences around the conference center was a local resident who had brought her parents and her dog. The resident stated that workers had been planting flowers for a year ahead of the summit, and added that a community worker had given her a big package of napkins as a gift after she agreed not to drive her car in the coming week. Shenzhen has halved fares this week on its extensive subway system to help clear the roads for summit buses.

According to recent reports, at the same time, however, residents are aware of occasional hassles. “Many friends who live around here proposal to travel outside the city because of the inconvenience of transportation — many roads will be closed to traffic,” noted the resident, who gave only her family name, Zhang. As is common at high-profile and high-security events in China, she was wary of giving her full name, which can be risky for Chinese citizens.

Few dare to express any misgivings, however, accepting the disruption with resignation. “Even if we’re unhappy about it, we can’t really say so,” remarked a resident surnamed Wang. “The government wouldn’t welcome our dissatisfaction.”.

While gatherings of world leaders always prompt extensive security, China’s efforts in Shenzhen are particularly intensive. Surveillance cameras are ubiquitous along streets in China and not noticeably more common this week in Shenzhen, but there are other, unobtrusive signs of the elaborate security effort underway.

According to recent reports, xiangmei Road, located near the main summit venue and lined with some of China’s costliest condominium towers, was much quieter than usual on Monday. A cleaner outside one of the towers who gave only her family name, Li, said that the family employing her has simply left town this week.

Sources indicate that police have been stationed in apartments on upper floors facing the conference center, drones have been prohibited and the remaining residents have received social media messages urging them to support the gathering, Ms. Li said.

“This place is usually very crowded,” she remarked, “but look how quiet it is now.”.

Ruoxin Zhang and Siyi Zhao contributed research.

    Breaking: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years.
    • Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge.
    • Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the organization exclusively told TechCrunch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.

    Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance.

    Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the organization exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.

    “The latest plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.

    In a recent development, molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.

    The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, stated Boyd.

    Sources indicate that the startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd stated. The firm says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.

    “We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” stated Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the firm’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”.

    According to recent reports, here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.

    Recent findings suggest that the basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd remarked no organization before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.

    Solving that problem changed the firm’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a byproduct.

    But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.

    The tech giant claims both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.

    The new factory, Boyd mentioned, “is really a milestone, not just for the organization, we think, but globally.”.

    Five EU states announce looks for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’.
    • Five EU member states have announced prepares to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
    • The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’.

    Five EU member states have announced prepares to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

    The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

    In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries mentioned “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an vital contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

    Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

    In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

    Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

    It has been revealed that the reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries remarked. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

    The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

    Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, stated it was “a huge breakthrough”.

    The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, noted: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”.

    Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”.

    Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

    It has been revealed that spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, mentioned on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

    The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She stated: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”.

    Industry observers note that alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, remarked it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

    Recent findings suggest that “On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

    Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

    Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” stated Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that as demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S.
    • The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading.
    • Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that as demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.

    The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

    Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.

    Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) remarked in an interview.

    Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.

    Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal stated. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.

    “Scale, diversity, and quality are vital aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal stated.

    Humyn Labs indicates it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.

    The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.

    Sources indicate that that growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal noted, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.

    Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups including Human Archive and BuildAI tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.

    Recent findings suggest that agarwal stated Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.

    Humyn Labs presently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said.

    Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a fresh social simulator powered by AI.
    • MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a upcoming social simulator powered by AI.
    • Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a upcoming game — and it’s built around AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a fresh social simulator powered by AI.

    MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a upcoming social simulator powered by AI.

    Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a upcoming game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.

    Sources indicate that the MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.

    Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”.

    According to recent reports, I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” claims Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow.

    Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting customers make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.

    Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.

    Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”.

    “We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.

    MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most key franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.

    According to recent reports, “It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?

    Sources indicate that imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he claims. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”.

    #23696. Breaking: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1319 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans.
    • The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
    • Industry observers note that the charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans.

    The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

    Industry observers note that the charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

    The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

    Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

    Industry observers note that the spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

    Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

    In a recent development, in confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

    If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

    According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

    In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

    It has been revealed that “The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik remarked. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”.

    Under the initiative, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

    The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

    The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

    One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

    In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

    The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

    It has been revealed that in order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers demonstrates that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

    On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU confirmed the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

    The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

    During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

    Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

    In a recent development, sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised key questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

    She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

    For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

    Strik stated: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”.

    Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, noted: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”.

    It has been revealed that in a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission mentioned the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

    Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

    It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

    Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

    #23694. Latest Update: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (897 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge.
    • Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures.
    • It has been revealed that business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.

    Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.

    It has been revealed that business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.

    Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also highlights where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.

    In a recent development, “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” remarked Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”.

    Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.

    In a recent development, unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

    It has been revealed that the San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.

    Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most crucial parts of a document.

    In a recent development, “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.

    According to recent reports, supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.

    In a recent development, unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.

    Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra noted, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.

    Industry observers note that presently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, prepares to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza.
    • Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
    • The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza.

    Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

    The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

    Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

    According to recent reports, it is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

    The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

    The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

    Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

    The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

    The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also confirmed sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

    It has been revealed that the Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

    Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

    Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”.

    In remarks addressed to Pillay, he mentioned: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”.

    In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”.

    He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

    Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

    In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

    It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

    The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

    The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

    Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

    Sources indicate that on Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its strategy to impose sanctions on the ICC.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.
    • Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.
    • For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

    Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

    For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands massive and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them.

    Sources indicate that most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them.

    In a recent development, something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case.

    In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon.

    The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care.

    Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a massive, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors.

    Sources indicate that with Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover.

    We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.

    In a recent development, for products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example.

    To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.

    According to recent reports, we cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

    This is the title for the native ad.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that one reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the organization’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom.
    • And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend.
    • According to recent reports, but Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that one reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the organization’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.

    And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter, which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.

    According to recent reports, but Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the manufacturer aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance latest data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, unveiled in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said.

    Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking. She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.

    Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the firm is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that “There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress remarked to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.

    Industry observers note that she pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also remarked this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.

    In a recent development, kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she noted, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.

    “The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”.

    One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products. Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the manufacturer’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations.
    • In a recent development, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable upcoming warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA.
    • Recent findings suggest that during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

    In a recent development, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable upcoming warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

    Recent findings suggest that during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” remarked a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog indicates three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

    Industry observers note that after the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

    It was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger.”.

    It has been revealed that this exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

    In a recent development, after five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

    In a recent development, testers reckon the UGV packs are ready for deployment and use in “a host of other missions, including food, ammunition and supply logistics and more,” according to the DARPA blog. More UGV pack hunting tests are scheduled for December, with a group of serving soldiers involved.

Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.

    はじめてDOOMで遊びます、自作のi486 PCで https://t.co/feosWgd6deNovember 9, 2026.

    According to recent reports, this project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

    Recent findings suggest that the enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.

    i486 CPU実験用ソケット完成 低クロックで動かなければ基盤発注する https://t.co/cXCnvPtkQ5October 24, 2026.

    Industry observers note that A significant milestone was reached on October 26, when the finished form of the breadboard system started to come into view, and the dev managed to get the CPU to blink an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].

    The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

    In a recent development, finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

    Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

    Sources indicate that alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

    Industry observers note that commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

    Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

    One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

    In a recent development, while PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

    Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed.
    • In a recent development, micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is.
    • The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some newly introduced evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the significant three memory chip manufacturers.

    In a recent development, micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”.

    The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was quickly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also stated that the three companies revealed the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”.

    Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

    The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

    Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.
