    Holiday gift guide 2026: 20 thoughtfully curated tech gifts that will charm and delight everyone on your list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating.
    • In a recent development, as the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating.
    • In a recent development, my selection process for this gift guide was entirely subjective.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating. But that’s not to say that there aren’t options out there. I often find that the best gifts are charming, focused devices with a touch of style. My selection process for this gift guide was entirely subjective. Almost everything on it is a gadget or design object with an element of tactile satisfaction for how it handles an everyday task. You won’t find a boring black rectangle anywhere on the list, and you shouldn’t have to think too hard about the soaring cost of memory. Apple: The First 50 Years by David Pogue Published to mark Apple’s half-century this year, veteran tech journalist David Pogue has marked the occasion with a hefty tome that serves as a biography of the company itself. Pogue conducted 150 interviews for the book, including figures like Jony Ive and Steve Wozniak, and the presentation benefits from hundreds of photos throughout. This is a book that’s worth owning in print. Twelve South Airfly SE Some airplane seatback screens support Bluetooth, but it’s not something you can always rely on when boarding a long-haul flight, as many screens still won’t connect to noise-canceling headphones. Twelve South’s AirFly SE is an inexpensive dongle that plugs into your seat’s headphone jack and transmits the audio to your cans. You’ll never need to use airline earbuds again. Sharge Flow Mini Go Sharge’s whole thing is designing utilitarian gadgets with a stylish twist, and the Flow Mini Go is one I can recommend to anyone who ever finds themselves running low on a charge. It has a 5,800-milliampere-hour (mAh) battery, 22.5-watt charging and a built-in cable, as well as an option to attach it directly to your phone’s USB-C port. Just as importantly, it’s only about as massive as a lipstick tube. Nothing Ear (a) At $79, Nothing’s Ear (a) model is my pick for affordable wireless earbuds. They sound great and look even better, especially if you opt for the construction-equipment-yellow pair. Even the charging case is cool, with a design inspired by medicinal blister packs. Logitech MX Master 4 Developer Edition If you know someone who uses a mouse all day but has never really thought about the actual mouse they’re using, the MX Master 4 might just change their life. The MX Master series has long been considered the leading productivity mouse due to its unique free-spinning scroll wheel, and the latest model adds a customizable haptic thumb panel that buzzes to confirm a shortcut. The fresh Developer Edition adds a “Hello, World” prompt and a reference to the Linux kernel’s release date. BOOX Palma 3 The Boox Palma 3 is an E Ink reader the size and shape of a smartphone, offering a convenient antidote to doomscrolling that you can take anywhere. Because it runs on Android, you can easily add your Kindle and Kobo libraries straight from the Google Play store. This latest version features a streamlined aluminum design and stylus support. 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard 8BitDo is best known for its excellent range of gaming controllers, and its first mechanical keyboard turned out to be just as haptically satisfying. Rolled out in versions that evoked the Nintendo Entertainment System and the Famicom, the lineup now includes models inspired by the Commodore 64 and the IBM Model M.. Each comes with enormous programmable buttons you can place next to the keyboard, making copying and pasting feel like a session at the arcade. Balmuda The Lantern Balmuda is a hip Japanese appliance maker best known for its minimalist steam toaster, but its equally obsessive take on the camping lantern may be a more practical gift. It has a single rotary dial that takes you from a warm, flickering candle-style effect at the low end to a brighter reading light when you turn it up. The light is diffused through a pipe for a soft glow, and its rechargeable battery means you can use it anywhere from the bedroom to the balcony. Analogue Pocket The Analogue Pocket feels like it came from an alternate universe where Apple designed the Game Boy. It has a gorgeous stripped-down design, an amazing high-resolution screen, and programmable hardware that has been tuned to provide the most authentic reproduction possible of Game Boy and Game Boy Advance games. The newer Analogue 3D does much the same thing for the Nintendo 64, if your gift recipient is more of a couch potato. Lego Game Boy Lego’s Game Boy is another meticulous reproduction of the Game Boy, but from a totally different angle. This kit is incredibly fun to build, making you build up the hardware from the circuit board level and work on the mechanisms of the satisfyingly squishy buttons and D-pad. As a display piece, you can swap out cartridges and lenticular screen inserts for Super Mario Land and The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening. Backbone One The BackBone One has been around for a while, but together with its Pro version, it still remains the top name in smartphone game controllers. And the proposition is more compelling than it used to be, with modern phones now powerful enough to run solid versions of high-end console games like Assassin’s Creed Mirage and Death Stranding. Backbone offers models with both PlayStation and Xbox controller layouts, depending on your preference. Aura Carver Mat Digital photo frames have been a clichéd throwaway gift for a long time, which is why Aura’s products stand out. The Carver Mat is a landscape, color-calibrated matte screen with a paper-textured border that automatically dims its lighting to match the ambient surroundings, making it feel much more natural than other digital frames. It can display two portrait photos side-by-side and even supports Live Photos from an iPhone. Kodak Charmera The Kodak Charmera hits on two recent trends: Labubu-style blind-box collectibles and the throwback use of lo-fi digicams. Each $35 box contains one of seven retro designs, and the tiny camera itself has several filters and frames. The image quality is not great, of course, but the Charmera is well-designed and well-named—it’s the perfect stocking stuffer. Fujifilm Instax Pal 2 If you like the idea of a tiny pocket camera but want the results to be a little more usable, Fujifilm has you covered with the $169 Instax Pal 2. It’s shaped like a vintage range finder, like many of Fujifilm’s more advanced mirrorless cameras—but even though it fits in the palm of your hand, it makes room for an optical viewfinder, a 1-inch display, a command dial for color effects, and a lever to swap between aspect ratios. Photos can be transferred directly to your phone or to an Instax Link printer. Peak Design Mobile Tripod The biggest problem with tripods is finding a way to take them with you. But here’s one you won’t even notice in your jeans pocket. Peak Design’s take on the mobile tripod folds three legs and a full-on ball head into a package that’s about 5 millimeters thick. It snaps onto your MagSafe-compatible phone with minimal obtrusion, and unfolds into a stand you can angle for group shots, video calls, or hyper-lapses. Native Union Pop cables and phone I’ve long been a fan of Paris-based Native Union, which puts out some of the most thoughtfully designed tech accessories around. Its coiled Pop Cables are particularly great, avoiding tangles and saving desk space—and now the company has revived its original Pop Phone, giving you an old-school handset to conduct your Zoom calls like you’re in an episode of Mad Men. There’s even a hang-up button. Xiaomi Portable Electric Air Compressor If you know anyone who rides a bicycle and plays basketball, this gadget might just change their life. For everyone else, it’s still worth keeping around—I’ve recommended it to countless friends. This USB-C-powered air compressor has modes tailored to all sorts of devices and displays the real-time pressure rating on its LCD screen. Nintendo Sound Clock: Alarmo Trust Nintendo to come up with a bizarrely useful take on something as mundane as the alarm clock. Anyone who shares a bed with a partner may consider it a hard sell to start each morning with sounds from Mario Kart or The Legend of Zelda. But the motion-sensing feature alone is a game changer for the groggy moments before getting up; the screen stays switched off until you turn your head to check the time. Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator Swedish design company Teenage Engineering first made its name through its iconoclastic synthesizers, and it sounds like the company might be moving on from that heritage. If that’s the case, now could be a good time to stock up on its $99 Pocket Operator series. It’s a range of exposed circuit boards with clicky switches, rotary dials, and monochrome LCD panels, all amounting to remarkably capable instruments. Yukai Engineering Nekojita FuFu In Japan, if you’re sensitive to hot food or liquids, you’re noted to have a nekojita—in other words, a cat’s tongue. Yukai Engineering is attempting to solve this condition with a tiny, rechargeable cat that attaches to the rim of your coffee cup or ramen bowl. Its internal fan drops the liquid’s temperature to a drinkable level in just a few minutes, and the cat looks cute in the process.

    #23614. The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2676 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain.
    • Massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain.
    • Sources indicate that this is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain. A crowd marches on the Interior Ministry and is driven back with bayonets. Students tear their school apart and barricade the doors; after hours of fighting with police, the army is called in. This is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement. Then, it was about bread and work; today, the cost of living and declining public services. Then, the industrial revolution added a backdrop of anxiety; today, another revolution in technology. Then, as now, students rebelled against the schools meant to form them. France is an extreme case of a global mood. Across the 30 countries tracked by Ipsos, the public opinion research firm, 62% say their country is on the wrong track. In the U.S., the figure is 73%; in France, it’s 89%. Edelman, a communications consultancy, finds in its annual trust survey that only 32% of people across 28 countries expect the next generation to be better off. In the U.S., it’s 21%, and in France it’s just 6%. These numbers are so bad that the social contract, that bedrock of civil society, is at risk. The problem isn’t a lack of change. It’s that the change underway isn’t the change people want. If the probable future is bleak, the most pragmatic thing to do is to take seriously the quest for improbable futures. Unfortunately, that is not a muscle most political or business leaders have built, trained as they are in playing the present game, not inventing entirely new forms of social and financial value. The case study method of business schools entrenches lessons from the past, not from the future; being trained in the logic of the law and finance does not naturally foster the kind of empathetic creativity that designs for what people want next. You can see it at this time of year, as companies draw up their annual plans: new columns in spreadsheets unwittingly determining a future that’s very much like the past, plus a bit. This year many companies will bake artificial intelligence into their forecasts to drive efficiency: a future that’s very much like the past, minus a bit. Is that really our highest aspiration for what people claim to be the most powerful technology ever created? And there is growing evidence that AI may deepen the problem. It favors the incremental over the radically new, making everyone’s ideas more alike. The probable future is not destiny The probable future is just one scenario among many. If we make different choices, we can design for something different: a plausible future, or more ambitiously, a possible future—or even, if we really allow ourselves to dream—a preposterous future. The field of strategic foresight describes this as the “futures cone.” Designed and built well, ambitious ideas start in the outer bounds, moving towards the center with diligent work. In 1956, Britain’s Astronomer Royal called space travel “utter bilge.” A moon landing became possible when the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth in 1961, plausible when John F. Kennedy put the weight of the U.S. government behind it, and probable when Apollo 10’s dress rehearsal succeeded in May 1969. One of humanity’s defining acts went from “bilge” to history in 13 years. History does not give us a road map to what’s next, but it does suggest some principles as to how to pursue the improbable. 1: Respond to a crisis with creativity While good times encourage incrementalism, the toughest moments open receptivity for the bold. The economist Milton Friedman went so far as to say that only a crisis produces real change, and that when it comes, “the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around.” The fragility of these moments can lead to great damage, or great progress. The Red Cross was inspired by the ravages of war. So were the Bauhaus, the German architecture and design movement, and the Paralympics. Today’s pervasive discontent does not preclude ambitious ideas; it creates the context for creation. 2: Take the first steps towards a preferable future The Schuman Declaration of 1950 proposed cooperation between France and West Germany for coal and steel. Two countries, two products. The aim was to make war between them “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” A united Europe was preposterous just five years after World War II, but as the declaration put it, “Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single strategy.” That first, discrete partnership began the process of bringing the preposterous towards the plausible. 3: Be willing to look ridiculous, together The most important principle is psychological. By their nature, improbable ideas are early, may be wrong, and risk ridicule. A prominent professor of futures studies, Jim Dator, in his second law of the future, goes so far as to say that any useful idea about the future should appear to be ridiculous. Which means its champions must be willing to be ridiculed. This is not natural in the meeting rooms, PowerPoint presentations and three-year plans where the future is articulated. It helps to assemble a group of people to withstand this phase. The 12 men who met in a London print shop in 1787 to end Britain’s slave trade had each other, and soon took their cause across England with lecture tours and petitions. This is where language, symbols, and rituals come in: visible signs of belonging and strength in numbers. The abolitionists had their Wedgwood medallion, with its image of a Black man in chains and its unforgettable motto, “Am I not a man and a brother?” The Red Cross had its emblem. From chants to T-shirts to lapel pins, the champions of the improbable need to see and find each other. What happened after the 1883 Parisian protests? While many of the French protestors of 1883 were expelled from school and others arrested, that same year, a 20-year-old of no great achievements, troubled by a nation still reeling from its defeat by Prussia, asked himself how he could help foster the character of a generation, such that civil society could thrive. He traveled across the Channel to England, home to the industrial revolution and an empire, and began researching its education system. He decided that playing sports was central to England’s development of citizens. It was where they learned respect, fair play, and collaboration within the context of rules. After nearly a decade of study and campaigning, this man stood up at the Sorbonne—just steps from the school the students had barricaded—and closed a speech by proposing the revival of the Olympic Games, dormant for some 1,500 years. The audience applauded, but almost nothing happened. The idea of uniting the world around sport was preposterous. So he took the first steps. In 1894, he slipped the Olympic revival onto the agenda of a congress on amateur sport. He convened 78 delegates, formed a 13-member International Olympic Committee, publicly declared their intent, invited others in, and championed the language and symbols of grand, shared endeavor. Within four years of his first sharing his preposterous, idealistic, pro-human idea, the first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896. The young man was Pierre de Coubertin, and he set in motion humanity’s greatest gathering, which draws billions of people into shared drama and values, from a moment of crisis much like our own. So for anyone drawing up next year’s plan, know that the gravitational pull towards the smart, expected future is strong. Ask yourself if there’s at least one possible, or even preposterous, idea on the table, how to take the first steps towards it, and who is going to hold the vision with you while it sounds absurd. The world is looking for new ways forward. What’s our de Coubertin moment? Sebastian Buck is a cofounder of ENSO, a future design company.

    Massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain. A crowd marches on the Interior Ministry and is driven back with bayonets. Students tear their school apart and barricade the doors; after hours of fighting with police, the army is called in.

    Sources indicate that this is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement. Then, it was about bread and work; today, the cost of living and declining public services. Then, the industrial revolution added a backdrop of anxiety; today, another revolution in technology. Then, as now, students rebelled against the schools meant to form them.

    France is an extreme case of a global mood. Across the 30 countries tracked by Ipsos, the public opinion research firm, 62% say their country is on the wrong track. In the U.S., the figure is 73%; in France, it’s 89%. Edelman, a communications consultancy, finds in its annual trust survey that only 32% of people across 28 countries expect the next generation to be better off. In the U.S., it’s 21%, and in France it’s just 6%. These numbers are so bad that the social contract, that bedrock of civil society, is at risk.

    Recent findings suggest that the problem isn’t a lack of change. It’s that the change underway isn’t the change people want.

    If the probable future is bleak, the most pragmatic thing to do is to take seriously the quest for improbable futures. Unfortunately, that is not a muscle most political or business leaders have built, trained as they are in playing the present game, not inventing entirely new forms of social and financial value. The case study method of business schools entrenches lessons from the past, not from the future; being trained in the logic of the law and finance does not naturally foster the kind of empathetic creativity that designs for what people want next.

    According to recent reports, you can see it at this time of year, as companies draw up their annual plans: new columns in spreadsheets unwittingly determining a future that’s very much like the past, plus a bit. This year many companies will bake artificial intelligence into their forecasts to drive efficiency: a future that’s very much like the past, minus a bit. Is that really our highest aspiration for what people claim to be the most powerful technology ever created? And there is growing evidence that AI may deepen the problem. It favors the incremental over the radically new, making everyone’s ideas more alike.

    The probable future is just one scenario among many. If we make different choices, we can design for something different: a plausible future, or more ambitiously, a possible future—or even, if we really allow ourselves to dream—a preposterous future. The field of strategic foresight describes this as the “futures cone.” Designed and built well, ambitious ideas start in the outer bounds, moving towards the center with diligent work.

    In 1956, Britain’s Astronomer Royal called space travel “utter bilge.” A moon landing became possible when the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth in 1961, plausible when John F. Kennedy put the weight of the U.S. government behind it, and probable when Apollo 10’s dress rehearsal succeeded in May 1969. One of humanity’s defining acts went from “bilge” to history in 13 years.

    History does not give us a road map to what’s next, but it does suggest some principles as to how to pursue the improbable.

    1: Respond to a crisis with creativity.

    In a recent development, while good times encourage incrementalism, the toughest moments open receptivity for the bold. The economist Milton Friedman went so far as to say that only a crisis produces real change, and that when it comes, “the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around.” The fragility of these moments can lead to great damage, or great progress. The Red Cross was inspired by the ravages of war. So were the Bauhaus, the German architecture and design movement, and the Paralympics. Today’s pervasive discontent does not preclude ambitious ideas; it creates the context for creation.

    2: Take the first steps towards a preferable future.

    It has been revealed that the Schuman Declaration of 1950 proposed cooperation between France and West Germany for coal and steel. Two countries, two products. The aim was to make war between them “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” A united Europe was preposterous just five years after World War II, but as the declaration put it, “Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single blueprint.” That first, discrete partnership began the process of bringing the preposterous towards the plausible.

    3: Be willing to look ridiculous, together.

    Sources indicate that the most crucial principle is psychological. By their nature, improbable ideas are early, may be wrong, and risk ridicule. A prominent professor of futures studies, Jim Dator, in his second law of the future, goes so far as to say that any useful idea about the future should appear to be ridiculous. Which means its champions must be willing to be ridiculed. This is not natural in the meeting rooms, PowerPoint presentations and three-year plans where the future is articulated.

    It helps to assemble a group of people to withstand this phase. The 12 men who met in a London print shop in 1787 to end Britain’s slave trade had each other, and soon took their cause across England with lecture tours and petitions. This is where language, symbols, and rituals come in: visible signs of belonging and strength in numbers. The abolitionists had their Wedgwood medallion, with its image of a Black man in chains and its unforgettable motto, “Am I not a man and a brother?” The Red Cross had its emblem. From chants to T-shirts to lapel pins, the champions of the improbable need to see and find each other.

    According to recent reports, while many of the French protestors of 1883 were expelled from school and others arrested, that same year, a 20-year-old of no great achievements, troubled by a nation still reeling from its defeat by Prussia, asked himself how he could help foster the character of a generation, such that civil society could thrive. He traveled across the Channel to England, home to the industrial revolution and an empire, and began researching its education system. He decided that playing sports was central to England’s development of citizens. It was where they learned respect, fair play, and collaboration within the context of rules.

    After nearly a decade of study and campaigning, this man stood up at the Sorbonne—just steps from the school the students had barricaded—and closed a speech by proposing the revival of the Olympic Games, dormant for some 1,500 years. The audience applauded, but almost nothing happened.

    The idea of uniting the world around sport was preposterous. So he took the first steps. In 1894, he slipped the Olympic revival onto the agenda of a congress on amateur sport. He convened 78 delegates, formed a 13-member International Olympic Committee, publicly declared their intent, invited others in, and championed the language and symbols of grand, shared endeavor. Within four years of his first sharing his preposterous, idealistic, pro-human idea, the first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896.

    The young man was Pierre de Coubertin, and he set in motion humanity’s greatest gathering, which draws billions of people into shared drama and values, from a moment of crisis much like our own.

    Recent findings suggest that so for anyone drawing up next year’s initiative, know that the gravitational pull towards the smart, expected future is strong. Ask yourself if there’s at least one possible, or even preposterous, idea on the table, how to take the first steps towards it, and who is going to hold the vision with you while it sounds absurd.

    Recent findings suggest that the world is looking for new ways forward. What’s our de Coubertin moment?

    #23613. Latest Update: China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up fresh hardware

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up fresh hardware

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • China's LineShine remains the world's highest-performing supercomputer, according to the 68th edition of the Top500 list published at SC26 in Chicago on Monday.
    • China's LineShine, installed at the National Supercomputer Center in Shenzhen, offers sustained FP64 compute performance of 2.198 FP64 ExaFLOPS in the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark at 42.22 MW.
    • Sources indicate that america's most powerful El Capitan supercomputer at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory relies on AMD's Instinct MI300A accelerated processing units (APUs), and the HPE Cray EX255a platform delivers 1.809 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 29.69 MW, which makes it significantly more power-efficient than its rival from China.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    China's LineShine remains the world's highest-performing supercomputer, according to the 68th edition of the Top500 list published at SC26 in Chicago on Monday. For the first time in decades, the supercomputer ranking saw exceptionally few additions despite unprecedented demand for high-performance computing hardware, as the vast amounts of compute resources deployed these days are destined for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers rather than traditional supercomputers.

    China's LineShine, installed at the National Supercomputer Center in Shenzhen, offers sustained FP64 compute performance of 2.198 FP64 ExaFLOPS in the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark at 42.22 MW. The machine relies on the homegrown LingKun platform with 304-core Armx9-based LX2 processors clocked at 1.55 GHz (13,789,440 cores in total) and the proprietary LingQi interconnect. Unlike the other four exascale-class supercomputers, LineShine does not use any compute accelerators and exclusively relies on CPUs, which is largely why it only gains 3.6X performance when moving from FP64 to mixed-precision data, which is lower than systems that use low-precision accelerators.

    Sources indicate that america's most powerful El Capitan supercomputer at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory relies on AMD's Instinct MI300A accelerated processing units (APUs), and the HPE Cray EX255a platform delivers 1.809 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 29.69 MW, which makes it significantly more power-efficient than its rival from China. The Frontier supercomputer at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, based on AMD's 3rd Generation EPYC processors and Instinct MI250X compute GPUs, achieves 1.353 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 24.61 MW. Meanwhile, Aurora at the Argonne National Laboratory, which uses Intel's Xeon CPU Max 9470 processors and Data Center GPU Max accelerators, offers 1.012 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 38.70 MW.

    All three American exascale supercomputers use HPE’s Cray EX platforms and Slingshot-11 interconnect.

    Germany’s Jupiter Booster at the Jülich Supercomputing Center, which employs Nvidia’s GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips, the BullSequana XH3000 platform, and Nvidia’s quad-rail InfiniBand NDR200 interconnect, delivers 1.0 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 15.79 MW and remains the most energy-efficient exascale supercomputer on the list.

    Remarkably, neither the 10 highest-performing supercomputers nor the 10 most energy-efficient machines have changed their positions since June.

    Only 27 new supercomputers (5.4% of all machines on the list) made it to the November edition of the Top 500, the lowest number since the project was founded in 1993. The most powerful newcomer is South Korea's Hanggang at the KISTI Supercomputing Center, which occupies the 12th position with 342.6 FP64 PFLOPS. The machine uses Nvidia's GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips and HPE's Cray EX254n platform. Hanggang also ranks eighth in the HPCG benchmark with 4.29 HPCG PFLOPS.

    Recent findings suggest that the aggregate HPL performance of the world's 500 highest-performing supercomputers increased by a modest 4.4% over the past six months to 19.57 FP64 ExaFLOPS. Nonetheless, it now takes a machine with 2.857 PFLOPS of sustained FP64 performance to qualify for the TOP500, up 7.3% from 2.662 PFLOPS in June. The performance of the systems ranked 50th and 100th rose from 49.85 PFLOPS to 55.81 PFLOPS (12%) and from 21.85 PFLOPS to 22.74 PFLOPS, respectively. Also, there are now 27 machines that deliver at least 100 PFLOPS of FP64 performance, up from 25 in June, whereas the number of supercomputers equipped with compute accelerators increased from 275 to 291 (58.2%).

    The historically low number of new entrants to the Top 500 is particularly noteworthy given the unprecedented scale of investments in advanced computing infrastructure these days. According to estimates by Epoch AI cited by the Top 500 authors, the amount of AI compute capacity added globally every quarter has increased by 2.5X per year. Essentially, the industry's priorities have shifted from construction of machines capable of solving exceptionally complex scientific problems to deployment of vast amounts of compute capacity for commercial AI workloads.

    In fact, the world's installed AI compute capacity already exceeds the equivalent of 15 million Nvidia H100 GPUs, according to Epoch AI. Furthermore, as of the fourth quarter of 2025, five major American hyperscalers accounted for an estimated 71% of the world's AI compute resources, much of which was deployed in massive clusters. While demand for advanced computing hardware is at an all-time high, it appears that the vast majority of upcoming hardware never makes it to the world's most known supercomputer ranking.

    #23612. FEMA has a cord-cutting problem

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1551 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    FEMA has a cord-cutting problem

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS).
    • In a recent development, on Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS).
    • It has been revealed that that’s bad news, especially when the next real emergency happens.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS). The test will cut into live broadcasts and cable reruns alike, and also be heard on radio stations across the country. However, anyone getting their TV fix from Netflix, Disney+, or any other streaming service likely won’t notice a thing. That’s bad news, especially when the next real emergency happens. According to recent Nielsen data, U.S. consumers are already spending half their TV viewing time with digital video platforms like YouTube and Amazon Prime. In other words: Half of America’s TV viewers are missing out on emergency alerts because they’re watching online instead. “It is vital that emergency alert systems adapt to changes in consumer technologies,” says University of Colorado Denver communications professor Hamilton Bean, an expert in public alert and warning systems. “Whether through streaming services, mobile devices, or IoT [Internet of Things], emergency alerts work best when they reach people where they are—at home, at work, or in public settings.” The federal government first began testing emergency alerts in the 1950s to warn citizens of a possible Soviet nuclear attack. Federal alert systems have been modernized multiple times since those early days, including an expansion to mobile phones in 2012. But in recent years, regulators and emergency management officials have struggled to keep up with rapidly changing media consumption habits and shifts in the TV business. This has led to confusing gaps in the Emergency Alert System. One example: Consumers who have switched their TV subscriptions from a cable company to an internet-based TV service like YouTube TV, Fubo, or Hulu + Live TV may also miss out on alerts. These so-called “virtual” pay TV operators don’t participate in the EAS, which means they don’t interrupt their programming to carry such warnings. But if a YouTube TV subscriber happens to be tuned into a local broadcast network like ABC or Fox, they may see the alert after all. Those channels are frequently ingested from local broadcast TV affiliates, which in turn do work with FEMA. In other words: YouTube TV subscribers who watch Dancing With the Stars on ABC during an emergency may get a warning, while those tuned into Bravo’s Southern Charm may be blissfully unaware of any impending danger. “Regardless of the other aspects of regulation, when it comes to public safety concerns, [traditional and internet-based pay TV services] should be on equal footing,” says John Bergmayer, legal director of the nonprofit technology advocacy group Public Knowledge. Virtual pay TV services already need to know a subscriber’s location to serve up local broadcast channels, which should help them target consumers with the right alerts. “And like cable, they have the technical capacity to both interrupt a program or to add some sort of crawl along the bottom of the screen,” Bergmayer says. Streaming services and their media company owners have generally resisted the idea of being forced to carry emergency alerts. In a 2021 regulatory filing, the Motion Picture Association, which counts Netflix, Disney, and Skydance among its members, declared that it would be “enormously technically difficult, if not entirely impracticable” to expand emergency alerts to streaming. One problem the industry association pointed to is the federated nature of America’s Emergency Alert System. While Tuesday’s test alert goes out nationwide, real warnings about wildfires or flooding are necessarily local. Requiring a streaming service like Netflix to relay those alerts would mean building out extensive monitoring infrastructure in every state. Some hope that the fresh Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) 3.0 broadcast standard, which brings modern technologies to antenna TV, will come to the rescue. In theory, modern TVs equipped with ATSC 3.0 tuners could interrupt a Netflix stream as soon as they receive an emergency alert via antenna. In practice, there’s no regulation in place to require this yet. Critics also fear that ATSC 3.0’s content protection technologies could hamper emergency warnings. In the end, the lesson from Tuesday’s test may be that emergency alerts can’t rely on just one technology. “There is no silver bullet,” says Art Botterell, author of To Warn Is Human: A Cultural History of Public Warning. Instead of trying to find a tech fix, he’d prefer that we invest in civic infrastructure and strengthen the bonds between neighbors so they can alert and help one another. “We need to facilitate that person-to-person sharing,” Botterell says. That, in turn, may also help people who happen to tune into the wrong TV show at the wrong moment.
